rv.q: This familiar show blows the roof off the Longacre Theatre, and makes a case for La Cage as a classic of American musical comedy.
The results, thankfully, are simply wonderful.
Their big, glitzy musical comedy hit of 1983 turns out to have a tender heart.
Is there a more appealing, entertaining argument for motherhood than La Cage aux Folles?
Yet the ladies of the chorus from “La Cage aux Folles” have never looked more appealing than they do in the warm, winning production that opened Sunday night at the Longacre Theater.
The new Broadway revival of 'La Cage aux Folles' is a sumptuous, sweet-natured production that does full justice to Jerry Herman's tuneful score and Harvey Fierstein's funny book.

Terry Johnson’s inspired revival of Jerry Herman and Harvey Fierstein’s musical, starring a happily mismatched Kelsey Grammer and Douglas Hodge (in a bravura Broadway debut), delivers the unexpected lesson that in theater, shabby can be not just chic but redemptive.
In the end, it's the tang of sweat under the greasepaint that invigorates this La Cage.

But since the scaled-down London import that opened last night lets us see Olivier-winning star Douglas Hodge in action, we'll take it. Kelsey Grammer may be the draw for local audiences, but the show is Hodge's alone.
Terry Johnson's London staging and its Olivier Award-winning star inject this musical with ingenious razzmatazz and a heartbreaking humanity.
Hodge, reprising his role from London, is simply sensational as Georges' better-spangled half.
They all seem to be having a swell time, as will you — so long as you can keep up with them.
Grammer is charmless and can’t sing, a problem for which I forgive the producers because the rest of the cast is so good.
By the end of this well-paced production, it's hard not to concur with the refrain of Albin's second-act number: The best of times is now.
Albin, meanwhile, might be a star, but he's not particularly talented - more like a second-rate music-hall performer.
It's easy to fall in love with this diminutive charmer of a production.
Now La Cage is a New York treat worth savoring.

While I wouldn't exactly use the exalted theatrical term 'ridiculous' to describe the newest Broadway mounting of La Cage aux Folles, it did strike me from time to time that director Terry Johnson's view of Jerry Herman and Harvey Fierstein's landmark musical tasted a bit like what the great Charles Ludlum might have done with the piece.
